articles.title: Nail polish colours and styles that are in vogue, and the ones we’re moving on from
articles.summary: As the seasons change, so does our polish.
articles.body: As the seasons change, so does our polish. Summer 2026 had its fair share of bright, playful manicures, from ocean-inspired turquoise and cerulean blue to sardine nail art that somehow made tiny fish on your fingertips look chic. But autumn calls for a slightly different mood.As wardrobes move from linen and bright colours to deeper tones and heavier textures, manicures are following suit. Fall 2026 is leaning towards chocolate browns, cherry reds, deep plums, teal, translucent syrup finishes and understated shimmer. Even the more playful summer trends are being given a darker, more sophisticated update.So, before you book your next manicure, here are the summer trends we can retire for now, and the colours and styles to try instead.The spring/summer trends we’re moving on fromTurquoiseTurquoise had a very good summer. The bright blue-green shade appeared everywhere, from clothing and accessories to hair and, naturally, manicures. It was playful, nostalgic and very much in keeping with the ocean-inspired beauty trends of the season. But now that summer is behind us, it is time to put the turquoise bottle away, at least temporarily.If you are not ready to let go, simply make it moodier. A deep teal is turquoise’s more autumnal cousin: darker, richer and easier to pair with the browns, blacks and jewel tones that tend to dominate fall wardrobes. It gives you the same blue-green family without looking quite so summery.Cerulean blueCourtesy to the sequel of The Devil Wears Prada, cerulean blue had its revival this year. It is an undeniably striking shade, but its bright, clear quality feels more suited to summer than the darker palette of autumn.Polka dotsPolka dots were everywhere this summer. On clothes, accessories and nails, the playful pattern had officially reached saturation point. So maybe, this season would be less of a nightmare for a trypophobe.But, if you are not one, you do not have to abandon the nail art altogether. Fall's version is less about repeating the same graphic motif across every nail and more about subtle details, darker colour combinations and finishes that add dimension. Think tiny dots against a deep cherry base (like snowflakes), rather than a bright, candy-coloured polka-dot manicure.Bright orangeOrange is one of those colours that refuses to leave quietly. It works particularly well through October, when Halloween gives it another lease of life.The neon and citrus versions that felt right in summer can start looking slightly out of place once autumn arrives. But, if your orange polish is still going strong, use it for Halloween or as an accent nail. Otherwise, move towards burnt orange, terracotta or a richer rust shade.Sardine nailsSummer 2026's most unexpected manicure trend was, quite literally, fishy. The sardine manicure took the year's fascination with tinned fish and coastal aesthetics all the way to our fingertips, with tiny sardines painted over sheer, nude, blue or pink bases. Vogue and Cosmopolitan both picked up on the trend as a defining summer manicure.It was quirky, fun and very much a summer trend. For autumn, however, it is time to let the sardines swim away.Fall/winter: what is in trend nowCherry red“Red for fall? Groundbreaking.”Red is hardly revolutionary for autumn, but there is a reason it keeps coming back. This season, instead of bright tomato or candy reds, look towards cherry, burgundy and oxblood.The easiest way to make the classic shade feel different is through nail art. If you loved summer's polka dots, keep the idea but change the palette: tiny white dots on cherry red can resemble snowflakes as winter approaches. Or simply stick to a glossy, classic cherry-red manicure.Soft syrupy nailsIf summer was about juicy, translucent nails, autumn is simply making them darker.Syrup nails use a sheer, glossy finish that allows some of the natural nail to show through. For fall, the technique is being reworked in shades such as caramel, amber, chocolate, black cherry and deep plum. The result is somewhere between a jelly manicure and a glossy lacquer: sheer, but noticeably richer.All things brownBrown has officially moved beyond being the supporting neutral. Chocolate, mocha and espresso are some of the season's most wearable nail colours, particularly in glossy finishes. Hailey Bieber's recent chocolate-brown chrome manicure has only added fuel to the trend.PlumFor anyone who considers burgundy too predictable but black too harsh, plum is the somewhere-in-between you might be looking for.Deep purple and plum shades are being highlighted as key fall colours. For a more understated version, try a sheer plum syrup manicure. For something more dramatic, go for an opaque, almost-black purple.Mother-of-pearlMother-of-pearl nails offer a subtle, pearlescent sheen rather than the chunky glitter of traditional metallic manicures. The look is a middle ground between a glossy chrome and a minimalist old-money manicure, making it a good option if you want something polished without committing to a dark autumn colour.For autumn, try the pearlescent finish over a milky white, pale pink, taupe or even a darker base.Cloud DancerThere is also one colour that refuses to follow the seasonal rulebook: Cloud Dancer, Pantone's 2026 Colour of the Year.The soft, creamy white has been a major manicure shade throughout the year and continues to work as a neutral as temperatures drop. British Vogue's 2026 nail trend report also identified variations of warm winter whites, creamy light colours and French-vanilla tones as enduring manicure choices.In other words, if you already have a bottle of Cloud Dancer sitting in your collection, there is no need to retire it with your summer polishes.Trends don’t change, they only evolveThe easiest way to update your manicure for autumn is not necessarily to buy an entirely new collection of colours. Sometimes, it is simply about changing the finish or the depth of the shade.Turquoise becomes teal. Bright orange becomes burnt orange. Summer reds and pinks become cherry or burgundy. A pale jelly becomes a chocolate syrup nail. Even summer's shimmer can be carried forward as a subtle pearl finish.So, if your favourite summer polish still has plenty left in the bottle, keep it. Just give it an autumnal remix. After all, nail trends may change with the season, but your nail-paint rotation does not have to.(ALl images from Pinterest and Canva)You use AI every day. articles.title: Why a Ramlila ground could be the perfect place to begin a relationship: Unconventional but deeply meaningful
articles.summary: Our parents’ and grandparents’ relationships often seem to belong to another era where people stayed together for decades, built lives around each other
articles.body: Our parents’ and grandparents’ relationships often seem to belong to another era where people stayed together for decades, built lives around each other and found love without the endless choices that define dating today. In an age of dating apps, situationships and relationships that can sometimes feel fleeting, permanence can seem increasingly elusive. So, what made those relationships last?Perhaps part of the answer lies in something as simple as where people met. Look back at old Bollywood films, and they offer a fascinating reflection of the social world of their time. People rarely met through dating apps or carefully planned coffee dates. They met at festivals, weddings, family celebrations, fairs, community gatherings, cultural programmes and religious events, occasions where the purpose was not necessarily to find a partner, but to come together and celebrate something larger than themselves.We may have more choices today, but perhaps there is something psychologically powerful about meeting someone while already sharing an experience of happiness, tradition or community. The setting becomes part of the memory , not just where you met, but what you were celebrating, whom you were with and how you felt at that moment.Could this be one reason why the old-fashioned meeting ground, the festival, the mela, the celebration or even a Ramlila still holds a special place in our collective imagination of romance? Perhaps finding love was never only about finding the right person. It was also about finding them in a moment that already meant something.Why is a mela is special?A good date ideally should be an experience where there is no pressure, conversations can flow easily, and both people feel connected. The melas provide exactly that. Unlike a fine-dine restaurant, the informal setting and the diverse crowd take away the pressure of having to behave a certain way.The conversation to know each other can be more meaningful and doesn’t have to be artificially orchestrated with pinterest prompts. Your conversations can even go beyond simply getting to know each other. They can revolve around food, culture, childhood or even how these spaces become examples of the dilution of class, caste and religious barriers. The sights, sounds and people around the mela can naturally give you more talking points, without having to think too hard about what to say next.The rides at the fair can give you a chance to discover traits that might otherwise stay unexplored. Who screams first? Who insists on going again? Who holds your hand when the ride gets scary? Between the adrenaline, playful teasing and those spontaneous “let’s do one more” moments, a simple ride can turn into a surprisingly easy way to break the ice. The ferris wheel can give you a moment to breathe and catch a romantic moment, a bumper car can tell you who’s more competitive. Even the question of whether your date is a front row person or a back bencher at the Dragon Boat ride can tell you more than you expected.From picking out silly souvenirs to debating about which ghost mask looks the scariest, there’s always something to react to. You get to know each other’s preferences: does she like jhumkas, or is she more of a bangle-stack girl? Does he like kurtas, or is still obsessed with toy cars? And when it comes to shopping, finding out who gets the better bargain can become something you both feel proud of or laugh about later. And if you end up buying each other a tiny keepsake along the way, you’ve got a little reminder of your first date to take home.Best places to experience the Ramlila mela around IndiaRamnagar, Varanasi- where the entire town becomes the stageFamous for its 31-day theatrical reenactment of the Ramayana, the Ramnagar Ramlila does not stay to the bounds of a ground. The entire Ramnagar turns into a stage with different parts of the town turning into Ayodhya, Janakpur, Chitrakoot, Panchavati and Lanka. The tradition dates back to the 19th century and is recognised by UNESCO as part of India's intangible cultural heritage. A walk through the historic town, while revisiting stories from ancient Indian scriptures, gives you and your date a chance to explore the past together in a way few experiences can match.Dates: September 25- October 25, 2026Where: RamnagarBest for- heritage and immersive experienceAyodhya, Uttar Pradesh- Ramlila in the land of RamExperiencing Ramlila at the birthplace of lord Ram gives it an unmistakable pilgrimage atmosphere. Being held at the river front, the Ramlila can be enjoyed with the ghats, temples, evening aarti and the festive atmosphere around Ram Ki Paidi. If you were planning to get the riverside experience along with a pilgrimage trip with your partner, this is the place for you.Dates: October 11 to October 20, 2026 from 07:00 PM to 10:00 PMWhere: Laxman Kila Ground (Saryu Riverfront, Ayodhya)Best for: spirituality, pilgrimage and festival photography.Delhi- for the big, buzzing Ramlila melaLike any other event, Delhi turns this one into a full-scale festival too. Ramlila Maidan and the Red Fort area are among the traditional centres, with elaborate sets, large crowds, performances and the much-awaited burning of Ravana's effigy. From Luv-Kush Ramlila at the Red Fort grounds, known for its theatrical presentation and elaborate sets to Shriram Bharatiya Kala Kendra, Mandi House offers a more structured theatrical experience. Delhi Ramlila scene offers a spot for all kinds of couples.Dates: October 11 to October 20, 2026 from 07:00 PM to 10:00 PMBest for: Grand productions, crowds, food stalls and carnival energy.Vrindavan, Uttar Pradesh for a Braj-flavoured celebrationVrindavan’s Ramlila is among the places specifically recognised by UNESCO for representative Ramlila traditions. Set in the wider cultural landscape of Braj, the place lights up with devotional performances, music and theatre deeply woven into the Braj tradition.Dates: October 23, 2026, to November 5, 2026Where: Shri Rangaji MandirBest for: devotional atmosphere and traditional performing arts.Madhubani, Bihar- Ramlila with a strong folk-culture backdropMadhubani is another UNESCO-recognised Ramlila tradition. An additional bonus while visiting this spot is that a visit here can also be paired with an exploration of the region's distinctive Madhubani/Mithila art. For art enthusiasts couples and people who like to explore local art traditions this can be an enriching experience.Dates: October 11 to October 20, 2026Best for: folk art, regional culture and an offbeat festival story.You use AI every day. Her last rites were scheduled for 10 am on Sunday.An Executive Magistrate has ordered the release of CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, co-convenor Saurav Das and party leader Ashutosh Ranka following their preventive detention by Delhi Police on Saturday.The three were detained after arriving in the national capital from Mumbai to participate in the party’s proposed ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ protest, which sought the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Delhi Police had denied permission for the demonstration, citing public safety, traffic management and law-and-order concerns. articles.title: Should You Buy Gold This Navratri and Dhanteras? Venus Is Retrograde
articles.summary: Navratri is one of the busiest times for jewellery shops in India.
articles.body: Navratri is one of the busiest times for jewellery shops in India. Many families buy gold during the nine days or on Dussehra, believing it invites Maa Lakshmi's blessings.But 2026 has a twist. Shukra, the planet of luxury and wealth, turned vakri (retrograde) on 3 October. It stays that way until mid-November, covering all of Navratri, Dussehra and even Dhanteras.So should you hold off? The answer isn't as simple as yes or no.What Shukra Vakri MeansVenus rules luxury, beauty, jewellery and comfort in Vedic astrology. When it moves backwards, one should exercise caution with new purchases in these areas. The concern is that items bought now may not bring the expected joy, or that decisions made in a hurry may need to be reversed later.This year, Shukra is vakri in Tula, its own sign. In Vedic astrology, a planet in its own sign is stronger, even when retrograde. So we don't see the effect as harsh. It's more like a phase for review than a red signal.Gold Isn't Ruled by VenusHere's the part most people miss. In Vedic astrology, gold is mainly linked with Jupiter (Guru) and the Sun. Silver, diamonds and fancy jewellery are more closely tied to Venus.So buying a gold coin or plain gold as savings isn't strongly affected by Shukra Vakri. Heavy designer jewellery, diamond sets or expensive luxury pieces are where we should be cautious.Navratri's Own StrengthTraditional muhurat rules also matter. Navratri days are considered auspicious on their own, and Dussehra is one of the few abujh muhurat days of the year. On an abujh muhurat, no separate auspicious time is needed for new beginnings.Best Days to Buy Gold This NavratriIf you do plan to buy, these days stand out:Thursday, 15 October: Guruvar during Navratri, Jupiter's own day. Good for gold as an investment.Monday, 19 October: Durga Ashtami and Maha Navami together. Many families consider this day highly auspicious for bringing gold home.Tuesday, 20 October: Dussehra, an abujh muhurat. Buy during the Vijay Muhurat if possible, between 1:59 PM and 2:45 PM in Delhi.What to AvoidSkip impulse buys at festive offers, especially on diamond and luxury jewellery. Read exchange and buyback terms carefully before signing anything.Also note that Venus comes very close to the Sun later in October. Panchangs mark this as Shukra Asta, a phase when marriage-related purchases and ceremonies are often postponed. If you're buying jewellery for a wedding, ask your family pandit about dates before committing.And remember, Dhanteras falls on 6 November this year, also during Shukra Vakri. The same thinking applies. Plain gold and silver coins for puja are fine for most families. Big-ticket luxury items can wait until Venus turns direct.Get the latest astrology news and horoscope updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: A family thought this Rodin sculpture on their piano was a copy for years; experts rediscovered the missing 1892 original and sold it for about $1 million
articles.summary: A small marble sculpture a family had kept on their piano for years, believing it to be a copy, has been confirmed as an authentic work by the French
articles.body: A small marble sculpture a family had kept on their piano for years, believing it to be a copy, has been confirmed as an authentic work by the French sculptor Auguste Rodin. The piece, called "Despair", sold at auction in France on Monday for €860,000 (£725,000; $982,000). The 28.5cm (11 inches) figure dates from 1892 and had disappeared after a sale in 1906. The Comité Rodin confirmed its authenticity following a six-week probe. Auctioneer Aymeric Rouillac described it as an "extremely rare" find and told the AFP news agency: "We have rediscovered it."Why did the family think the sculpture was a copyAccording to BBC News, the family approached the French auctioneer Aymeric Rouillac, and he and his team then spent months investigating the origins of the piece. In March, Mr Rouillac brought the sculpture to the Comité Rodin, a research group dedicated to studying the works of Rodin. The Comité Rodin confirmed the sculpture's authenticity after a six-week probe. Mr Rouillac described the piece as an "extremely rare" find. The work was then put up for auction and sold on Monday. BBC News reports that "Despair" is a work by Rodin from 1892.Why had Rodin’s sculpture disappeared after the 1906 auctionThe Comité Rodin found that the sculpture had disappeared after being sold at an auction in 1906. Mr Rouillac spoke about the discovery to the AFP news agency. He said: "We have rediscovered it." The family's sculpture was an original piece. "Despair" was originally modelled by Rodin as part of his series of figures for The Gates of Hell. The Musée Rodin says that the figure is a depiction of sorrow. The Musée Rodin also states, as reported by the BBC, that the sculptor created other versions of the figure after it was positively received. The family's marble piece is one of the works confirmed by the Comité Rodin following its investigation.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Sponges 'lift off' Chesham town tapestry's 50 years of grime
articles.summary: The artwork is cleaned and restored to "safeguard it for decades to come", a town council says.
articles.body:
More than 50 years of grime and "engrained dirt" has been painstakingly lifted off from a tapestry using "many, many make-up sponges".

The Town Tapestry was embroidered by members of Chesham Arts Society to showcase scenes of the Buckinghamshire town.

The town council said it was sent to Zenzie Tinker Conservation, in Brighton, which carried out more than 30 hours of cleaning and restoration work "to safeguard it for decades to come".

It has now been re-hung in the council chambers inside a bespoke frame with acrylic glazing.

The work of art was created "by dedicated community embroiderers", the council said.

An inspection found it was "soiled and grubby with some moth damage" and it was sent off to be cleaned and repaired.

The council shared an image of "previously white sponges" that were now blackened with dirt.

The work was originally painted by local artists before it was embroidered by residents.

It features the Market Hall, that no longer exists, and The Bury , which was about 70% destroyed in a fire on 1 October.

Zenzie Tinker confirmed "many, many sponges" were used as it was "incredibly soiled".

She said it was also heavily stained with nicotine as it had hung in council chambers before indoor smoking was banned.

"We all really loved the embroidery for its skilled execution and now slightly vintage feel and particularly liked it as a piece of community art", she said.

"It is so important to help preserve these types of textile artworks because textiles are very vulnerable to damage from dust, light, pollution and handling particularly when not framed.

"Stories told through textiles - as the far more famous Bayeux Tapestry is currently illustrating, can be really important social and historical documents that everyone can relate to.

"The conservation of the Chesham embroidery will be one we remember really fondly.

"Often it is the preservation of less valuable, family items that give both the clients and our conservation team the greatest pleasure to conserve."

The council said: "The front and back of the embroidery were vacuumed to remove surface dust, before the face of the textile was carefully worked over with make-up sponges to lift off soiling and ingrained dirt."

It was then carefully wiped "with a specialist microfilament material and a 50:50 mix of denatured alcohol and deionised water".

The conservation work was funded by a grant from the Pilgrim Trust.

articles.title: Beyond Jaisalmer's sand dunes: 6 Rajasthan experiences worth planning this winter
articles.summary: Rajasthan’s regal history, along with its desert landscapes, is best explored when the weather is pleasant and comfortable.
articles.body: Rajasthan’s regal history, along with its desert landscapes, is best explored when the weather is pleasant and comfortable. Rajasthan is one of the states in India that should not be missed when travelling around the country. The state is packed with culture, history and magnificent architecture, featuring vibrant, colourful cities, local handicrafts and a rich folk culture. Winter is the perfect season to experience the beauty of Rajasthan. From forts and palaces to lakes and gardens, Rajasthan has something for every kind of traveller.Let this be your guide to getting the best Rajasthan experience this winter.1. Tiger spotting at Ranthambore National ParkAn underrated travel experience for wildlife lovers awaits you in the royal state. This winter, swap the palace corridors for jungle trails and head to Ranthambore National Park. The reserve is known for its Royal Bengal tigers, but that isn’t all. The entire safari experience, which can be booked through the official Rajasthan Forest Department portal, involves sightings of varied wildlife, including sambar deer, wild boars and sloth bears.The national park is centred around the historic Ranthambore Fort near Sawai Madhopur. The fort itself has a deep history, with royal women said to have performed jauhar (self-immolation) when Alauddin Khilji laid siege to the fort in 1301. The fort is also recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site under Hill Forts of Rajasthan.2. Hot-air balloon ride over RajasthanThe streets of Rajasthan are quite narrow and provide a limited view of the city. While forts set atop the Aravalli hills provide beautiful views of the skyline in some places, a hot-air balloon ride over Rajasthan offers a bird’s-eye view of the landscape. This experience has become increasingly popular among young couples, photographers and international tourists.October to April is generally a suitable period for outdoor activities in Rajasthan, although the operating season for hot-air balloon rides varies by location and operator. The most popular places for this activity include Jaipur and Pushkar. Sunset flights may be available depending on the operator, while early-morning flights are also common. To ensure a smooth experience, book in advance with a reputable, authorised operator. Moreover, wear comfortable clothes with sufficient layers, as it can get chilly at dawn and dusk. Most importantly, do not forget to enjoy the experience and take a bunch of pictures.3. Escape to the hills of Mount AbuMount Abu is situated at an elevation of approximately 4,000 feet and may surprise you if you are expecting only sand dunes and dry landscapes in Rajasthan. Mount Abu is the state’s only hill station, where you can relax amid cooler air, forested hills and peaceful views.The hill station is home to Guru Shikhar, the highest peak of the Aravalli range, which houses the Guru Dattatreya Temple. The place is most famous for the Dilwara Jain Temples, which are adorned with intricate carvings and are among the important pilgrimage sites of the Śvetāmbara Jain tradition. Other attractions include boating on Nakki Lake and visiting Toad Rock.4. Heritage walk through Jodhpur’s Blue CityImagine an entire city offering Instagram-worthy pictures while giving you a heritage experience. In Jodhpur, the real fun lies in getting lost in the old city’s blue-painted lanes, browsing spice shops and stopping for a plate of quintessential mirchi vada or a glass of lassi. The iconic Mehrangarh Fort and Jaswant Thada are the landmark spots to visit in the city. But the trip is incomplete without exploring the local markets, where colourful textiles, handcrafted juttis and traditional jewellery make tempting souvenirs.5. Jawai, the land of leopardsThe rugged granite hills of Jawai are an offbeat wildlife destination in Rajasthan’s Pali district. Its safaris are renowned for sightings of free-roaming leopards that live alongside local communities. It is an exemplary place to experience the coexistence of humans and animals, although access and movement are subject to local conditions and wildlife-related guidelines. The place is also frequented by migratory birds that gather around the Jawai Dam. It is the perfect destination if you want to experience rural life in Rajasthan.6. Sajjangarh — Monsoon PalaceThe Monsoon Palace, also known as Sajjangarh Palace, is a hilltop palace built by Maharana Sajjan Singh. Originally planned as an astronomical centre, the palace was later used as a monsoon retreat and hunting lodge. It is a splendid sight, offering spectacular views of Udaipur’s skyline and the surrounding areas.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
